title: Long counts gave no clear repeated decrease in snow richness contrasts in four North American feeder samples in 2001-2005 and 2021-2024
abstract: We tested whether long bird counts had a smaller deep-snow richness contrast than short counts. We used 126,232 FeederWatch checklists in eastern and western North America in 2001-2005 and 2021-2024. Four separate models controlled site-winter, regional week, hour category and the exact half-day schedule. Long counts meant more than eight hours; short counts meant less than one hour. Long minus short estimates were -0.227 and -0.554 species in the two eastern samples and -0.152 and +0.549 in the two western samples. Only the later eastern four-test interval was below zero: -0.978 to -0.130 species. An added state or province cluster check kept only that interval below zero. Thus a clear decrease did not repeat across the four samples. Only five of 11,069 selected site-winters had both extreme duration categories in both snow states. All four planned fits restricted to these winters failed the minimum support rule. Broad effort categories, selected sites, missing reports, shared weather and possible changes in feeder attendance limit inference. A duration contrast does not identify a detection mechanism or a causal effect of snow. The source records fully overlap a prior campaign study. The package gives original follow-up code, aggregate evidence, two figures, exact source hashes and a raw rebuild that keeps external records outside the publication. Air pollution and human-caused climate effects were not tested.

display.caption: Long minus short snow richness contrasts in four samples. Left: intervals adjust for four primary tests. Right: duration profiles at the full four-half-day schedule, with marginal 95% intervals. These are recorded-richness associations, not causal effects.

Only five of 11,069 selected site-winters had both extreme duration categories in both snow states. Counts show weak support for a complete within-winter comparison. The axis is linear from zero to one and logarithmic above one.
